name: Electric toothbrush whitening heads

lead: Whitening heads are replacement heads for electric toothbrushes, sold to lift surface stains.
No studies of the heads themselves were found; electric brushes overall show modest plaque benefits.

paras: Polishing bristles or pads mechanically remove surface stain. They do not bleach internal tooth colour.
Heavy brushing pressure can harm enamel and gums. Heads are advised to be replaced about every three months.

lead: Electric toothbrush whitening heads are replacement brush heads marketed for use with powered toothbrushes to remove surface stains and make teeth look whiter. They typically differ from standard heads in bristle layout or a polishing cup or pad.

Electric toothbrushes in general are described as removing more plaque and reducing gum inflammation than manual brushes in a 2014 Cochrane review, though the review's authors questioned the clinical importance of the difference [1]. Mechanical brushing mainly addresses surface (extrinsic) stains; it does not bleach the tooth interior [2].

paras: Powered toothbrushes are oscillating-rotating, sonic or ultrasonic [1]. Manufacturers sell heads labelled for whitening, often with polishing elements, and many sonic brushes include a whitening mode [1].

sections.h: What brushing can and cannot change
paras: Surface stains from coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco can be reduced by cleaning, while intrinsic discolouration within the tooth is not removable by cleaning and is what bleaching targets [2]. Whitening toothpastes give modest, gradual gains [2].
Brushing too hard can damage enamel and gums, and some brushes include pressure sensors [1]. Manufacturers advise replacing heads about every three months [1].
No studies found specific to whitening heads. Broader research on electric versus manual brushing is summarised in a Cochrane review [1].
